brief.t: Started in Chennai in 1979 as Shriram Transport Finance, lending to truck owners (often for used trucks) that banks did not serve. The Shriram Group was founded by R. Thyagarajan.
In December 2022 Shriram Transport Finance and Shriram City Union Finance merged to form Shriram Finance, adding two-wheeler and small-business (MSME) loans to vehicle loans.
Japan's MUFG Bank bought a 20% stake for about ₹39,618 crore (deal announced Dec 2025, completed 8 Apr 2026), one of the biggest foreign investments in Indian financial services.
Parag Sharma became MD & CEO on 5 Dec 2025 (he was earlier the CFO); the board has re-appointed him for five years from 13 Dec 2026. Umesh Revankar is Executive Vice Chairman.
Q2 FY27 profit rose 59% to ₹3,677 crore and AUM reached ₹3.29 lakh crore, but management trimmed FY27 AUM growth guidance to 15–17% and bad loans in some areas rose a little.

timeline.t: Shriram Transport Finance incorporated in Chennai to finance commercial vehicles.
Merger with Shriram City Union Finance (and Shriram Capital) creates Shriram Finance.
Parag Sharma takes over as MD & CEO from Y.S. Chakravarti; MUFG Bank signs deal for a 20% stake.
MUFG deal completed (₹39,618 cr); two MUFG nominees join the board. AUM crossed ₹3 lakh crore by March 2026.
Q2 FY27: profit ₹3,677 cr (+59%), AUM ₹3.29 lakh cr; FY27 growth guidance cut to 15–17%.

model.how: Shriram Finance borrows money (public deposits, bonds/NCDs, bank loans, overseas borrowing, securitisation) and lends it to small truck owners, farmers, small businesses and two-wheeler or gold-loan customers, many in rural and semi-urban India. It earns the gap between its lending rate and borrowing cost.
flow: Raises money: deposits, NCDs, bank loans, ECBs
Lends: vehicles, MSME, gold, two-wheeler, personal loans
Profit after costs and bad-loan provisions

points: NBFCs like Shriram lend to people and small firms that banks often find too risky or too small, especially in rural and semi-urban India.
Foreign banks are buying into Indian lenders: MUFG's ₹39,618 cr deal for 20% of Shriram is among the largest such investments in Indian financial services.
Vehicle sales grew strongly in 2026, helping vehicle lenders, but credit costs (bad-loan provisions) are being watched closely.

Gross Stage 3 4.65%, Net Stage 3 2.31%; net interest margin 9.52%.

numbers.say: Shriram Finance earned ₹3,677 crore in Q2 FY27, up 59%, with AUM of ₹3.29 lakh crore, and its new 20% shareholder MUFG gives it stronger capital and cheaper funding potential.

rivals.note: Rivals differ by product: vehicle loans (Chola, Mahindra Finance), consumer and MSME loans (Bajaj, Tata Capital, L&T Finance), and gold loans (Muthoot).

network.local: Shriram has deep roots in Tamil Nadu and South India, and more than half its customers are in rural and semi-urban areas, so many roles are in branches and field teams across small towns.

employer.note: From Great Place To Work announcements (Feb and Apr 2026). The FY26 BRSR reports 76,241 permanent employees at 31 Mar 2026.

csr.t: Shriram's CSR focuses on the transport community: scholarships for children of truck-driver families (Class 8–12), mobile medical units giving free check-ups to truckers, and two-wheeler repair skill training with job support.

glossary.NBFC: Non-Banking Financial Company: a lender regulated by the RBI that gives loans but cannot take savings or current account deposits like a bank.
glossary.AUM: Assets Under Management: the total loans an NBFC has given out and not yet been repaid. The main size measure for a lender.
glossary.Disbursements: New loans paid out to customers in a period.
glossary.Net profit: What is left after all costs, provisions and taxes. The company's final earnings.
glossary.Net Interest Income: Interest earned on loans minus interest paid on borrowings. A lender's main earning.
glossary.Net interest margin: Net Interest Income as a % of loans or interest-earning assets. Shows how profitable lending is.
glossary.Gross NPA: Loans not repaid for 90+ days (called 'Stage 3' loans by NBFCs), as a % of all loans.
glossary.Net NPA: Bad loans after subtracting the money already set aside (provisions) for them. Lower is better.
glossary.Stage 3 assets: Loans that have stopped paying for 90+ days. NBFCs report Gross and Net Stage 3, similar to banks' NPA.
glossary.Credit cost: Money set aside for bad loans, as a % of average loans. Lower means fewer losses.
glossary.Capital adequacy ratio: The lender's own capital compared with the risk in its loans. RBI requires NBFCs to keep at least 15%.
glossary.Provisions: Money set aside from profit to cover loans that may not be repaid.
glossary.Borrowings: Money an NBFC raises from banks, bonds (NCDs), commercial paper and, for some, public deposits, to lend onward.
glossary.Cost of funds: The average interest an NBFC pays on its borrowings. NBFCs usually pay more than banks, so a strong credit rating matters.
glossary.Credit rating: An agency's grade (e.g. AAA) of how safely a company can repay debt. Higher ratings mean cheaper borrowing.
glossary.Upper Layer NBFC: The largest and most important NBFCs, named by the RBI under its scale-based rules. They face bank-like rules and must list on the stock market within 3 years.
glossary.Return on assets: Net profit as a % of average total assets. Shows how well a lender earns on what it owns.
glossary.Dividend: Part of the profit paid to shareholders, per share.
glossary.Attrition: The % of employees who leave in a year. Also called employee turnover.
glossary.RBI: Reserve Bank of India, which regulates banks and NBFCs in India.
glossary.KYC: Know Your Customer: checking a customer's identity before giving a loan.
glossary.MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises: small businesses that lenders serve.
glossary.Cross-sell: Selling an extra product (like insurance or a second loan) to an existing customer.
glossary.Co-lending: A bank and an NBFC lending together: the NBFC finds and services the borrower, the bank funds most of the loan.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first sells its shares to the public.
glossary.BRSR: Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report: an official yearly report on people, environment and governance that big listed companies must publish.
glossary.Securitisation: Selling a pool of loans to investors to raise money; the lender gets cash now and investors get the loan repayments.
glossary.Preferential issue: New shares sold directly to a chosen investor (like MUFG) at a set price, instead of to the public.
glossary.Used vehicle finance: Loans to buy second-hand trucks, cars or tractors. Higher rates than new-vehicle loans, and Shriram's traditional strength.
glossary.Gold loan: A loan given against gold jewellery kept as security.

Finance.tip: Know AUM, Gross vs Net Stage 3, cost of funds and credit cost, and the company's latest profit.

Marketing.tip: Think about reaching first-time and small-town borrowers through dealers, branches and mobile.

HR.tip: NBFCs hire many field and branch staff. Ideas to cut early attrition and train people fast will impress.

Sales.tip: Expect role-play: 'Sell me a two-wheeler loan' or 'Convince a shopkeeper to take a business loan.'

Operations.tip: Show you understand KYC, loan turnaround time, collections and how automation reduces errors.

Finance.q: Why is Shriram's net interest margin (about 9.5%) so much higher than a bank's?
Finance.a: It lends to riskier small borrowers (used vehicles, MSMEs) at higher rates; the margin pays for higher credit costs and operating costs.

Finance.q: What does MUFG's 20% stake do for Shriram's finances?
Finance.a: It added about ₹39,618 cr of equity, strengthening its capital and potentially improving ratings and borrowing costs.

Finance.q: Q2 FY27 profit rose 59% but the stock fell. Why?
Finance.a: Investors focused on the cut in AUM growth guidance to 15–17% and a rise in credit costs; profit growth also benefited from the new equity.

Marketing.q: How would you market gold loans to Shriram's existing truck-owner customers?
Marketing.a: Use branches and field staff they already trust, stress quick cash and low paperwork, and offer it as a short-term working-capital option.

Marketing.q: How can Shriram attract younger, digital customers?
Marketing.a: Through its app, simple two-wheeler and personal loan journeys, and regional-language digital campaigns in small towns.

HR.q: Shriram has 75,000+ employees, many in small towns. How would you reduce early attrition?
HR.a: Hire locally, give clear career paths, quick training on products and collections, and recognise field staff often.

Sales.q: Sell a used-truck loan to a first-time truck owner.
Sales.a: Understand his routes and income, show an EMI that fits his earnings, and explain fast approval and branch support nearby.

Operations.q: How would you speed up loan approvals across 3,225 branches?
Operations.a: Standard digital KYC and document checks, clear turnaround-time targets, and central checks for risky cases only.

Other.q: What is Shriram Finance known for?
Other.a: Commercial and used vehicle loans to small operators, now also MSME, gold, two-wheeler and personal loans.

interview.why_us: Shriram Finance serves truck owners, farmers and small businesses that many banks overlook, and has grown into a ₹3.29 lakh crore lender. With MUFG now a 20% shareholder, it is entering a new growth phase in gold, MSME and digital lending. I want to learn credit and customer work close to real India.

gd.t: Should foreign banks own big stakes in Indian NBFCs?
gd.for: Brings stable capital, cheaper funding and global practices (e.g. MUFG–Shriram).
gd.against: Risk of foreign influence on lending priorities; profits flow abroad.

gd.t: Are NBFCs better than banks at serving rural India?
gd.for: Local knowledge, faster decisions, used-vehicle and informal-income lending.
gd.against: Higher interest rates and higher bad loans; banks have cheaper deposits.

avoid: Calling Shriram a bank: it is an NBFC and cannot offer savings accounts.
Saying MUFG owns or controls Shriram: it holds about 20% and is classed as a public shareholder.
Mixing standalone and consolidated profit figures.
